questions.question: A client has A1C 6.5% but reports several episodes of severe hypoglycemia each month. What is the best interpretation?
choices: The A1C proves the regimen is safe
The A1C does not reveal dangerous glucose lows; the plan and goal need individualized review
The lows can be ignored if the average is below 7%
A1C directly counts every low-glucose episode
questions.explanation: A1C reflects an average, not variability or hypoglycemia. Recurrent severe lows require prompt review of the regimen, monitoring data, and individualized goals.

questions.question: A client using CGM feels shaky and sweaty, but the sensor displays 115 mg/dL during a rapid glucose change. What should the RN do?
choices: Dismiss the symptoms because the sensor is above 70 mg/dL
Check a blood glucose value using the approved meter or hospital protocol and assess the client
Give scheduled insulin based on the sensor without reassessment
Turn off all glucose monitoring
questions.explanation: Interstitial CGM readings can lag or be inaccurate during rapid changes. Symptoms that do not match the sensor require a blood glucose check and clinical assessment.

questions.question: An alert adult who can swallow has glucose 62 mg/dL. Which first response follows a common hypoglycemia protocol?
choices: Give 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate and recheck glucose in about 15 minutes
Give a large insulin correction dose
Wait an hour without treatment
Give food by mouth only after the client loses consciousness
questions.explanation: For a person who can safely swallow, a common approach is 15 g of rapid carbohydrate, then glucose reassessment in 15 minutes, repeating if still low and following the individualized protocol.

questions.question: A client receiving insulin is unconscious and cannot swallow. Which action has priority?
choices: Place juice in the client's mouth
Protect the airway, call for emergency help, and give prescribed glucagon or IV glucose under protocol
Wait for spontaneous recovery
Administer the next prandial insulin dose
questions.explanation: Severe hypoglycemia with impaired consciousness requires emergency support and nonoral glucose rescue. Giving oral intake to an unsafe swallow risks aspiration.

questions.question: A hospitalized client with type 1 diabetes becomes NPO for a procedure. Which plan is safest?
choices: Stop all basal insulin without an order
Coordinate glucose monitoring and an adjusted basal plan with the prescriber while withholding meal-linked insulin when the meal is absent
Give the full prandial dose despite no meal
Stop all glucose checks until the procedure ends
questions.explanation: Type 1 diabetes requires ongoing basal insulin even when intake is interrupted, though doses may need adjustment. Meal-linked insulin and monitoring must be coordinated with the NPO plan.

questions.question: A person taking an SGLT2 inhibitor becomes ill with vomiting, abdominal pain, and deep breathing, but glucose is only moderately elevated. What should the RN consider?
choices: Ketoacidosis may occur without very high glucose and needs urgent evaluation
DKA is impossible unless glucose exceeds 600 mg/dL
The symptoms confirm simple hypoglycemia
No assessment is needed because the sensor reading is modest
questions.explanation: SGLT2-associated ketoacidosis can present with less marked hyperglycemia. Vomiting, abdominal pain, and deep breathing are warning signs needing urgent ketone and acid–base assessment.

questions.question: Which monitoring pair best helps detect diabetic kidney disease over time?
choices: Serum sodium alone and urine color
Estimated GFR and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio
Hemoglobin alone and a pulse check
A single fasting glucose without follow-up
questions.explanation: Both eGFR and urine albumin are needed because albuminuria can show kidney injury even before substantial loss of filtration, and trends guide follow-up.

questions.question: A person with diabetes reports a new foot ulcer with spreading redness and warmth. What should the RN recommend?
choices: Prompt clinical evaluation for infection and limb risk
Wait for the next annual foot visit
Walk barefoot to keep the wound dry
Use a sharp tool at home to remove surrounding tissue
questions.explanation: An ulcer with spreading inflammatory signs may progress quickly, particularly with neuropathy or ischemia. Timely assessment and coordinated wound and vascular care are needed.

questions.question: Which discharge check best confirms a new insulin plan is usable?
choices: The prescription was transmitted electronically
The client demonstrates the correct device and dose, explains meal timing and low-glucose actions, has supplies, and knows the follow-up plan
The RN verbally lists the medicines once
A family member says the client will probably remember
questions.explanation: Teach-back and demonstration reveal whether the person can carry out the exact insulin, monitoring, hypoglycemia, and follow-up plan with available supplies.

questions.question: A noncritically ill hospitalized adult has persistent hyperglycemia, but the team proposes a target of 80–110 mg/dL. Which concern should the RN raise?
choices: Very tight hospital control can increase hypoglycemia risk; the target should follow the individualized inpatient plan
The target is automatically best for every inpatient
Glucose monitoring can stop after the first normal value
A1C alone sets the hourly inpatient goal
questions.explanation: For many noncritically ill adults, current guidance favors a less stringent inpatient range when safely achievable. Overly aggressive targets raise hypoglycemia risk and require individual review.
